source.title: Rethinking the Role of Text Complexity in Language Model Pretraining
source.authors: Dan John Velasco; M. T. Roque

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present. No apparent truncation or garbling affects the study results.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures perplexity across model sizes and evaluates downstream results at multiple sizes, but does not reproduce or fit the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The study compares held-out perplexity across six model sizes and reports downstream evaluations. The perplexity results are described in text and shown in Figure 1, but the size-by-size perplexity values are not tabulated. The study does not fit a power law or report loss predictions. No result rows are included for scaling laws cited from other work.
record.test_reason: The study is about text complexity, not scaling. It trains six sizes (28M–500M) on a fixed 2B-token corpus and reports downstream scores at each size. That bears weakly on V6 in a small, data-limited setting. No power law is fitted, there is no compute or token sweep, and loss values are figure-only, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that simplifying text barely affects fine-tuning or linear-probe performance. In zero-shot tests, complex text helps Entity Tracking, EWoK and ARC-Easy, while simplified text helps BLiMP-supplement. They note that fine-tuning confirms larger models do better, and attribute the 500M zero-shot drop to limited data (2B / 1.71B tokens).
record.recipe_differences: The study compares models trained on parallel human-written and simplified corpora over six sizes; it does not reproduce the original parameter/token/compute sweeps or fit scaling equations.
record.method_sensitivity: Perplexity degradation differs between fwedu_hw and fwedu_simp. Downstream outcomes vary by task and pretraining corpus; several zero-shot scores are lower at 500M than at 256M.

fits_no_version.finding: Perplexity degradation as models shrink is larger on human-written text than on simplified text, with a sharp drop at 28M on fwedu_hw.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size-dependence of loss interacts with training-data complexity; smaller models lose less on simpler text.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the First BabyLM Workshop
record.problems: The paper does not tabulate size-specific perplexity values or fit a scaling law. The tested size range is 28M–500M, the corpora contain around 2B tokens, and the authors note limited data and model capacity as possible bottlenecks. The downstream results cover a limited set of tasks and report a drop at 500M on several zero-shot evaluations.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap required prioritizing the perplexity comparison, the reported seven-task fine-tuning averages, and three zero-shot metrics illustrating size and corpus differences. Omitted zero-shot results are BLiMP, BLiMP-supplement, EWoK, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag (Tables 4–5); individual fine-tuning task scores and linear-probing results are also omitted (Tables 3 and 6).

untested.parts: There is no power-law fit, no tabulated loss values, only about 1.2 orders of magnitude in parameters, and token count is fixed (a bottleneck for the larger models).
Not tested at all; the Chinchilla ratio is used only to justify dataset size.
The shape is varied only incidentally (the 500M model has 40 layers, the others 30), with no fixed-parameter comparison.
No predictive fit of downstream score against scale or loss; only the direction of change across six sizes.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling is incidental here: there is one seed for pretraining, a fixed data budget, and a narrow size range. Treat V6 verdicts as weak, and read the 500M drops as a data-bottleneck condition. The Table 5 caption says every 500M model drops relative to 256M; this holds for Table 5 tasks, but BLiMP-simp 500M (72.60) is slightly above 256M (72.53). Omitted tasks such as BLiMP, EWoK and HellaSwag are declared in rows_left_out; the text says BLiMP and EWoK improve with size.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports perplexity trends over 28M–500M models but does not test whether loss follows a power law, over several orders of magnitude, or when parameters, tokens, and compute are not bottlenecks.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
The study does not vary depth, width, or architecture at a fixed parameter count.
The study uses English text pretraining and does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as training regimes for a power law.
The study evaluates downstream task scores at different model sizes, but does not fit a predictive relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
The study does not compare scaling-law exponents or test how fitting choices affect them.

rows.subject: Causal LMs, fwedu_hw (size sweep aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared held-out perplexity across model sizes; degradation is defined relative to the 500M model.
rows.measure: Perplexity degradation as model capacity decreases
rows.note: The text says fwedu_hw models degrade faster as capacity decreases, with a sharp drop at 28M. The plotted size-specific values are not given in the text.
rows.check: This is held-out loss against parameter count, so it is V1's measure. Values are figure-only, the range is under 1.5 orders of magnitude, the larger models are data-bottlenecked and no fit is made, so power-law form can't be read. The corpus-complexity interaction also belongs in fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Full-model fine-tuning, seven-task average, both corpora, 28M–500M
relationships.reason: Averages rise monotonically with size: 67.4→71.2 (hw) and 67.1→70.8 (simp). The gains are small, and there is no fit (R5–R14).
relationships.display_finding: Seven-task averages increased monotonically from 67.4 to 71.2 on hw and 67.1 to 70.8 on simp, without a fitted scaling relationship.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot ARC-Easy and PIQA with fixed ~2B tokens, going from 256M to 500M
relationships.reason: Scores rise up to 256M (R35, R47, R48), then all four series drop at 500M (R37, R38, R49, R50). The authors blame a data bottleneck.
relationships.display_finding: Scores peaked by 256M and declined across all four series at 500M, which the authors attributed to a data bottleneck.

relationships.reason: The hw series is non-monotonic and falls to 20.81 at 500M (R25). The simp series stays near chance with no clear size trend (R18, R26).
relationships.display_finding: The hw series fluctuated and fell to 20.81 at 500M, while the simp series remained near chance without a clear size trend.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
